title: Greedy: Gas Station
oneLiner: Find the station to start a full loop from: if the tank ever goes negative, no station up to here can be the start.
keyTakeaway: Two facts give an O(n) answer. If total gas < total cost, no start works. Otherwise, run a tank from a candidate start; whenever it drops below zero at station i, every station from the candidate up to i fails too, so the next candidate is i + 1. The last candidate standing is the answer.
explanation:
n gas stations sit on a circular road. Station i has gas[i] litres, and driving from station i to station i + 1 (wrapping from the last back to 0) burns cost[i]. You start with an empty tank at some station, fill up there, and drive round. Return the index of the station where you can start and get all the way round, or -1 if there is none. The problem promises at most one answer. For gas = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], cost = [3, 4, 5, 1, 2] the answer is 3.

Simulating a loop from every start is O(n^2). Instead look at diff[i] = gas[i] - cost[i], the net change in the tank at each step. First fact: if the sum of every diff is negative, you burn more than you can ever collect, so return -1. If the sum is zero or more, some start works (that's a theorem; the scan below finds it).

Second fact, the greedy step. Start at candidate s with tank = 0 and add diff[i] for i = s, s + 1, and so on. Suppose the tank first goes negative after station i. Could any station k between s and i be a better start? No: you reached k from s with a tank of zero or more, so starting at k with an empty tank gives you no more fuel than you had, and you'd still run dry at i. So skip them all: the next candidate is i + 1, with the tank reset to 0. One pass over the stations, keeping total and tank, gives the answer in O(n) time and O(1) space.

Why don't you need to loop back round after picking the last candidate? Because the total is non-negative and the stretch before the candidate summed to a negative amount, the stretch from the candidate to the end must carry enough surplus to cover it.

The visualization shows diff = gas - cost for the example. The tracker is the tank from the current candidate.

Station 0: tank = -2, below zero. No station from 0 to 0 can be the start. Next candidate: 1, tank reset to 0. (total so far -2)
Station 1: tank = -2, below zero. No station from 1 to 1 can be the start. Next candidate: 2, tank reset to 0. (total so far -4)
Station 2: tank = -2, below zero. No station from 2 to 2 can be the start. Next candidate: 3, tank reset to 0. (total so far -6)
Station 3: diff 3, tank = 3 >= 0. Candidate 3 survives. (total so far -3)
Station 4: diff 3, tank = 6 >= 0. Candidate 3 survives. (total so far 0)
total = 0 >= 0, so a full loop exists, and the surviving candidate is station 3. Answer: 3.

recognitionSignals: A circular route with gains and costs, asking for a valid starting point.
A running total that must never drop below zero, where a failure lets you rule out a whole stretch of starts at once.
A brute-force O(n^2) "try every start" with an obvious O(n) total check sitting next to it.
gotchas: Reset the tank to 0 when you move the candidate; don't carry the negative amount forward.
Check the grand total separately (or at the end). The candidate after the scan is only valid when total >= 0.
The new candidate is i + 1, not s + 1: every station between s and i is ruled out too.
confusableWith: Maximum Subarray (Kadane's algorithm, this track) uses the same "a negative running sum is never worth keeping, restart after it" move.
Prefix Sums: the tank from start s at station i is a difference of two prefix sums, and the answer is the station just after the lowest prefix sum.

complexity.note: One pass keeping the grand total, the tank since the current candidate and the candidate itself. Each failure rules out a whole stretch of starts, which is why there is no inner loop.
